newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock index futures end mostly lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock index futures end mostly lower.

text.p: U.S. stock index futures finished mostly lower, with June Standard & Poor's 500s setting session lows in late active trade.
June S&Ps fell below 841.90 with the authority they lacked during earlier tests at that critical support area, they said.
The next downside target rests at 832.00 to 832.50, fitting in with the scenario that the market could correct to the 800.00 area within the next two months, some said.
Traders noted that sell-stop orders were hit at 841.60 after retail continued to sell against local buying. Losses in the afternoon were initially countered by dealer buying.
Some dealers were decent buyers of June as it sold off when T-bond futures closed at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT, they said.
However, one dealer remained a strong seller throughout the day, selling about 2,000 contracts and fueling speculation of asset allocation into U.S. bonds from U.S. stocks.
The premium between June S&Ps to the cash narrowed to a level needed to spark arbitrage sell programs, but traders reported little program activity in the afternoon.
Arbitrage sell programs needed a premium of 0.70 points. To touch off arbitrage buy programs, June S&Ps needed to rise to a 2.30 point premium against cash, traders said.
However, June S&Ps opened well below fair value, which was at 1.30 points on Wednesday, and struggled to adjust their premium against cash S&Ps all day.

Light bargain-hunting in some bellwether technology stocks also lifted S&P futures for most of the morning. June popped above the pivot point at 846.05 but failed to carve out a fresh session high on several stabs at the upside. Meanwhile, the selloff in the technology sector resumed.
"We are really just a status quo market going into Friday's employment number," another S&P futures analyst said about the overall U.S. stock market.
Average estimates for U.S. May nonfarm payrolls growth were put at to 219,000, from April's 142,000. The U.S. unemployment rate is forecast to rise to 5.0 percent, versus 4.9 percent in April.
U.S. average hourly earnings for May are expected to rise 0.4 percent, from a drop of 0.1 percent in April, while the average U.S. workweek is seen at 34.7 hours, from 34.6 in April.
Any signs that the U.S. labor sector remains strong will raise expectations for a Federal Reserve tightening at the next policy meeting on July 1-2, traders said.

At the end of pit trade, June S&Ps were off 1.05 at 842.10, NYSE Composites were off 0.25 at 441.00, KCBT Value Lines were steady at 758.00, and Nikkeis were up 15 at 20,550. ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750)) E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
